utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today there is a hearing on the 11 bis motion. Prosecution appearances first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, esteemed guests. For the Prosecution, Susan L. Somers, to my right Ms. Marie Tuma, Mr. Aleksandar Kontic, and Ms. Lise-Lotte Karlsson, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Somers. For the Defence, Mr. Mrksic's Defence first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to all those in the courtroom. Appearing for Mr. Mile Mrksic attorney Miroslav Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. For Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning my learned friend. Appearing for Miroslav Radic, attorney Borivoje Borovic of Belgrade and his legal assistant Ms. Gerasimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Then for the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Appearing for Mr. Sljivancanin Novak Lukic, attorney from Belgrade, and Mr. Momcilo Bulatovic also from Belgrade, and our assistant, Maja Dokmanovic from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Then the government of Serbia Montenegro and the Government of the Republic of Croatia are invited. Could we have the appearances first of the Government of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LJAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all participants today. The delegation of Serbia and Montenegro includes me as the president of the Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, Mr. Djeric, legal advisor, Mr. Svetoslav Obrenovic, the legal advisor of the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then for the Government of the Republic of Croatia. Or is there -- is there a misunderstanding? It's -- you introduced yourself as the president of the Council for the Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and your name was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LJAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Rasim Lajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Lajic. Yes. In the translation and on the transcript it did not appear in full, so I was confused. Then for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all. My name is Zeljko Horvatic, I am a professor emeritus of Zagreb University and a special advisor of the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Croatia, and I represent the Republic of Croatia before this Court. With me is Mr. Jaksa Muljacic, the assistant to the Minister of Justice, and Ms. Irena Cacic from the embassy of the Republic of Croatia in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Horvatic. Before the first break I'd like to before an opportunity to the Office of the Prosecution and then to three Defence counsel to make further missions to what has already been submitted in writing. After the break I'd like to give an opportunity to the -- both governments involved to add what whatever they want to add to the written submissions and the Bench might have some questions then for the parties and the governments. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Given the number of persons opposite me as it were, not in the literal sense but in the courtroom, I will try to be brief to enable those persons to field any questions that the Chamber -- that the Bench may have. I do want to point out that in this instance which is unusual in some of the 11 bis filings, there are two states that have been included in the request. Pursuant to Rule 11 bis (B) which authorises the Prosecution for the Bench proprio motu to make the request, the Prosecution has pursuant to 11 bis A invoked both sections (i) and (ii) -- I'm sorry (i), and then in an exceptional set of circumstances has included the Government of Serbia and Montenegro because of ongoing related trials which are set forth in paragraphs, I believe, 34 and 36 of our filings of February 8th, just to make it clear as to why there are in fact two parties. The normal designation would be for the territory where the crimes were committed. Further, the Prosecution wishes to emphasise that pursuant to its submission of the 28th of April, referring you to paragraph 30 of that submission with the footnote, the materials it intends and deems appropriate to submit are set forth there. Nothing further. There were some additional indications in the Defence's further submissions about a continued engagement by the Prosecution above this and beyond this and this is not contemplated nor appropriate in our view. The extensive record that is available also to the parties -- I'm sorry, to the governments from a case although did not reach a case of decision, which is the Dokmanovic case, nonetheless presents it is our submission a wealth of potential facts which could prove to be useful and certainly makes the transition to prosecuting this case in whichever jurisdiction the Bench deems it appropriate should it order referral. It will facilitate the Prosecution of the case. We do want to emphasise that in sharp contrast to the existing prosecutions now in Belgrade, this case does involve command responsibility and some other crimes, of course, that are -- that perhaps were not covered in the criminal codes that may have dominated at the time of the offences. Command responsibility issue is indeed a major focal -- it is a focal point of the case and the Chamber in its deliberations will have to consider how best that aspect of the Prosecution can be handled given all positions on what laws may be applied. Certainly the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has been enriched recently with command responsibility determinations, and yet we want to be sure that the character of the Prosecution remains effectively intact should referral be granted. And the level of the accused which we deem appropriate for referral nonetheless has to be factored in with the nature of the allegations. The issue of monitoring is -- appears to be well in hand. The reports that have come out concerning the abilities of the countries to carry on war crimes trials are available to the public and to the Referral Bench, and I'm sure that any further inquiry can be made of the -- the states if they speak on this issue or if the Chamber wishes further information on the issue of the process of monitoring as has been taking place in their domestic jurisdictions on war crimes cases. It is pointed out that both territories do have war crimes chambers, and we want to also indicate that any inquiries by the Bench may also want to be as to the nature of cooperation between the various states on issues of documentation, witness protection which we think is something that of course must be very much factored in. There appears to the Prosecution to be a bit of a dispute as to the number of Croatian witnesses who have gone to the Serbian proceedings, and I would ask the Chamber perhaps to inquire into that of the parties. Croatia has one opinion. The Serbian Montenegrin representatives have another. At this time I would not go further but would reserve if the Chamber -- if the Bench will permit as issues may come up in the course of the hearings today if we may seek any possible further comment at a later time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Next would be Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As I have been assigned the role of speaking first on behalf of the Defence team, I wish to inform you that the Defence teams with a view to presenting their views concisely and succinctly divided the topics to be presented. Some topics may be dealt with at greater length than others, but I wish to assure you that the Defence teams will abide by the time frame assigned us. The Defence has put forward most of its standpoints in its two submissions, so we would like now to present some new arguments dealing with particular issues and responses to the positions of my learned friends in their submission, and the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia. Bearing in mind the Defence submissions, one may conclude that in the view of the Defence, this case meets the requirements for the application of Rule 11 bis (C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Defence would like to point out, however, that it is crucial for the rights of the accused to be respected, that the decision made by Your Honours with respect to Rule 11 bis (A), this is extremely important, and these are two issues, is the issue of extradition and the issue of a fair trial. The Defence has already put forward its standpoint that all three solutions are provided for in Rule 11 bis (A) and that they are of equal importance and make it possible for more than one state to aspire to have the case transferred to that state. However, when reaching a final decision on this issue, Your Honours should bear in mind the issue of extradition, which the Defence has raised in its response to the Prosecution motion for referral. The Defence submits that were the case to be referred to the judiciary of the Republic of Croatia and the accused handed over to the authorities of that state, the universally accepted principles of extradition would be seriously breached and those governing re-extradition, and this has already been put forward in the Defence submission. Whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for one second. One of the basic underlying issues is whether the defendants voluntarily came to The Hague or whether they were brought as a result of the force exercised upon them by a state. Could you please address that issue also as one of the vital underlying matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will answer your question right away. Mr. Mile Mrksic voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal in The Hague, and he arrived here escorted by members of the organs of the state security of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He voluntarily surrendered, and the state merely mediated in his transfer to The Hague and his surrender to the organs of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we will get a response for the other defendants on this issue. So he came by his own free will although escorted by state officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He came of his own free will after expressing his desire to surrender. And in view of the law on cooperation that had been adopted, he surrendered himself to the authorities of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a very simple question. If you want to come by your own free will, he could have travelled to The Hague himself as well or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He arrived to The Hague on his own. We bought an air ticket and travelled on a commercial flight, but escort was provided by security organs, which doesn't change the fact that he came to The Hague of his own accord, of his own free will. He had not been arrested prior to that. But since according to the previously adopted law on cooperation with the ICTY, it was the state that was the vehicle of cooperation with the Tribunal. Mr. Mrksic expressed his will to come to The Hague, and the state simply organised his transfer to the organs of the ICTY. If you're asking me if there was any coercion brought upon Mr. Mrksic, no, there hasn't been any. His surrender was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that I hear from other counsel on the position in respect of their clients?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this part of the proceedings, each Defence team will present the position of their own clients separately because we are not sure they're all in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I got the impression that your client wanted to share or at least to address the Court. As you know, it's usual in this type of proceedings that counsel represents the -- I would say primarily the accused person who is the subject of a 11 bis request. If there's -- would be any need to consult with your client, please do so, and if not, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I need just a moment for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I should like to pick up where I left off. So could Mr. Mrksic who surrendered voluntarily be transferred to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia despite the fact that at the time when he surrendered the Rule 11 bis envisaged that a case could be referred only to the jurisdiction of the state from which he had come and once the legislation of that state prohibits extradition of its citizens, especially when the authorities of that state are prepared and willing to try him. In this connection, we should take a look at the way this issue was resolved in Article 146 of the fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians during the war. In para 2 of this article, it is stipulated that "each contracting party will be under obligation to detect persons suspected of having committed or having ordered grave violations and to bring them before their own courts regardless of their nationality and citizenship. The contracting parties will also be in a position, if they wish so, under the conditions stipulated in their own legislation to transfer them to another contracting party that has a vested interest in such a trial if such a contracting party has in its possession a sufficient amount of evidence to try that person. Bearing in mine the general rule according to which a state may decide whether it is going to try perpetrators of crimes itself or will transfer them to another state, then the obligation envisaged by Article 29 of the Statute of the ICTY, in the view of this Defence, would be an exception that could only be justified in case of a transfer to the International Tribunal. In case of referral to the State of Croatia, there has been actually an extradition in two stages with the mediation of the ICTY, and the very provisions of Article 29 of the Statute do not provide for transfer of suspects or indictees by the Tribunal to third states. Therefore, in the view of this Defence, this would be an extradition rather than a transfer of an indictee because, in our mind, transfer of the accused is possible only in one direction, to the International Tribunal. Corroboration for possible transfer or extradition to the Republic of Croatia and its authorities cannot be found even in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY itself as pointed out in the submission of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro, para 52. Looking at the generally accepted rules on extradition and re-extradition, this Defence team respectfully suggests to this Chamber to request clarification of this issue from the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro during this session. Thus, in the view of this Defence, the provisions of 11 bis (A) give the Chamber an alternative, that is to make a decision that would not be in violation of generally accepted principles governing extradition and the fundamental right of the accused to a fair trial. The positions of the Defence concerning possibilities of an independent and impartial trial before the courts of the Republic of Croatia or the state union of Serbia and Montenegro will be dealt with at a later stage by my learned colleague, Mr. Lukic. One of the issues asked by the Referral Chamber of the parties was which law should be applied to a trial in this case if it were to be referred to national jurisdictions. The Defence stands by its previously expressed position that pursuant to Article 2, para 4 of the basic Criminal Code, it is necessary to apply the law which is the most favourable to the accused, which is the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1993. We wish to emphasise that in the view of this Defence and in view of the previously cited legal provisions, that is -- or that would be the right decision, although it is the privilege of the Referral Chamber to decide. And finally, I would like to say a few words about the submission of the representatives of the Republic of Croatia in which they expressed their views in response to the questions of the Referral Chamber regarding possible advantages of trying the accused in the Republic of Croatia rather than in Serbia and Montenegro. As to the conclusion that the case should be tried in the state where the crimes were be committed, we expressed our position in our written submission under the heading "Issue of forum delicti comisi," so we shall not repeat that position here. The Defence cannot agree with the other conclusions either, namely that the laws are more favourable on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Bearing in mind that the special chamber for war crimes in Belgrade is currently trying a case against 17 accused who are charged with ordering and committing crimes against prisoners of war perpetrated at the Ovcara farm at Vukovar between the 20th and 27th November, 1991, and bearing in mind the fact that this Defence team has been closely following the proceedings, we are able to express our view that the greatest number of the witnesses and most of the material evidence regarding documentation from that time are located precisely in the state union of Serbia and Montenegro. The indictments under which the aforesaid proceedings are taking place cover the same events as the indictments brought by the ICTY wherefrom referral is requested. If we compare these two indictments, we can see that the first and the second accused who, under the Belgrade indictment, are charged with ordering the crimes are in fact persons whom the OTP cites in their indictment as participants in a joint criminal enterprise together with the accused Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin. In both these indictments, the victims are the same, persons from the Vukovar Hospital, with the proviso that the Belgrade trial is dealing with those who issued orders for this crime, whereas the indictment under discussion here is an indictment where the Prosecutor claims that these persons are responsible as participants in the joint criminal enterprise under Article 7(1) of the Statute and as superior commanders under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Concerning the trial in Belgrade and the claims expressed by the representatives of Croatia regarding the ability of witnesses to come to the trial, we will hear more from my learned colleague, Mr. Borivoje Borovic. However, before that, I should like to make a few remarks about one fact, namely the confidential submission regarding protective measures filed by my learned friends from the OTP on the 17th of December, 2004, and the 31st of January, 2005. After the Defence expressed its views, that is after the response of the Defence, the Trial Chamber issued its decision on the 9th of March, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate the concern of my learned friend from the Prosecution, and I wish to thank her. But I will stop here for a moment only to ask the Honourable Chamber to pay attention to the request of the OTP for protective measures of the 31st of January, 2005, attachments A and B included, and the response of the Defence to this motion, paras 13, 14, and 15, as well as the decision of the Trial Chamber including confidential annex A. I thank you, Your Honours, most sincerely. My learned friend Borivoje Borovic will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Dear colleagues, I will present the views of the Defence which will include some observations and comparative analysis of the positions of the representatives of Croatia and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Prosecution has requested certain protective measures for a certain number of witnesses. This motion has partially been granted, and the Defence believes that if the case were to be transferred to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Special Chamber for War Crimes in Belgrade, these protective measures will remain in force in keeping with Article 14(A) of the law on proceedings in war crimes cases, which we will hereinafter refer to as the law on war crimes. In Article 5 of this law, we read that the measures for the protection of witnesses ordered by the ICTY shall remain in force. In its submission of the 28th of March this year, the Defence -- or, rather, the Prosecution expressed its view that some other witnesses will also need protective measures. Before this special chamber for war crimes in Belgrade this principle has been upheld. And in view of all the positions expressed in our submissions, special protective measures for victims and for witnesses would not even be necessary. In proof of this claim, the Defence has presented cases Ovcara and Severin currently under review in Belgrade, and in paragraphs 46, 47, and 51 we elaborated on this. The OTP has in its submission given a review of the legislation in Croatia. From this we see that although the legislation does provide for protection of witnesses, which is a very important issue which will recur in all these proceedings, practice has shown that many of these protective measures for witnesses are still at the stage of development or are failing to be applied. In the special report on the situation of Croatian legislation that was under review by this Tribunal of the 26th of April, 2005, there are passages regarding the negative atmosphere in the courtroom, coercion of witnesses, and other negative phenomena. So far we have seen 500 cases of trials in absentia in Croatia against Serbs. In the case of Petar Sailovic, who was convicted in absentia after spending some time in prison, we saw that eventually it was decided that it was a case of mistaken identity. This Chamber also knows that out of a total of 28 accused, there were 14 Serbs convicted in absentia. In this report on page 23, item 2, we read that during the trial monitored by the mission, witnesses claimed that they were being threatened before interrogation, before proofing, rather, in cases Hubelic and Gavron. This is also the right moment to correct a slight error in our own submission. When we spoke about the witness Milan Lever the case of the so-called Gospic Group where we stated in our submission that it was a witness of Serb ethnicity. Milan Lever is in fact a Croat who was supposed to be an important witness in the Gospic trial, and we have information that he was also to be an important witness in the Norac before this Tribunal. However, before he ever appeared before the court, he was killed. In the report on page 25, item 3, we read special passages about testimony of witnesses from the former Yugoslavia. This report says that the greatest number of witnesses were afraid of going back to Croatia to testify. On page 23, item 1 regarding Zoran Banic, a Serb tried before the parish court in Zadar, it is said that several journalists disturbed the closing arguments of both the Defence and the Prosecution, and it was very difficult to restore peace in the courtroom. Another important case is very important. The parish court in Vukovar -- the county court in Vukovar, that is. With the explanation of the county court in Vukovar regarding the possibility of transfer of these cases, we read that there is a plan to try these persons in absentia. That involves Judge Ante Zekovic, and the state defender Bozidar Piljic, who received information on the 24th of March this year that there is an active case in the county court in Vukovar. And they are trying precisely our accused. This is an example of the court which has priority over the national court of Croatia. In fact, this county court was challenged for trying a case in which the national court has priority, and the response was that the accused should be defended by lawyers who are appointed, by appointed Defence counsel. We are, therefore, arguing that it is a unique case where we have a parallel trial before the county court in Vukovar and the ICTY against the same accused. I will not exaggerate if I say that in the view of this Defence, this is a gross violation of the Rules of the ICTY. The support for this claim that the Rules of the ICTY are being violated is to be found in the application of the rules of the ICC. In Article 21, para 1, it says that the same accused cannot be tried on the same charges in the Republic of Croatia and before the ICTY at the same time. The Croatian state has not yet enacted a law which would apply also to the ICTY regarding this same issue. However, the judiciary of the Republic of Croatia would have first of all to abide by their own constitution, the Croatian constitution, which does uphold the principle non bis in idem. As for the immunity of witnesses, that is potential witnesses in this -- in the event that the case is transferred to Serbia and Montenegro, in our joint submission of the 28th of March of this year, in para 49, we stated that it was precisely Article 14 on the law on war crimes that is cited, and it says verbatim, Article 14 of the law says: "A person who is located abroad cannot be detained, imprisoned or criminally prosecuted for a crime committed earlier in the Republic of Serbia." In criminal cases from para 2 of this law, this victim or witness concerned will be adequately protected. With regard to immunity of witnesses should this case be referred to the Republic of Croatia, according to the ICTY Statute and the Croatian law, Article 49, para 2, it provides that Article 28 of the said law is to be applied to the ICTY in Article 28 on taking over cases from the ICTY by the Republic of Croatia. However, in para 5, Article 28 of the law of the application of the Statute of the ICTY, it says that the Croatian government may conclude a separate agreement with the ICTY. The Defence of these accused has not found any information that there is a special agreement, and thus we have arrived at the view that there is no immunity for potential Serb witnesses who are to testify in Croatia. The comment by the OTP of The Hague Tribunal on the fact that Serbia and Montenegro have no special law on the protection of witnesses and that such a law is yet to be enacted, but in response to that, the Defence wishes to point out that the bill which exists has been tabled in parliament. However, in commenting on this, the Defence in its submission and now in our oral presentation of arguments, we wish to remind everyone that not only Article 109 of the Law on Criminal Procedure but also Article 173, paragraph 1, Article 292, and Article 504 of the Law on Criminal Procedure deal with this issue. Also, Article 15(M) of the law on organised crime, as well as the law on war crimes, Articles 11 and 14. All these deal with issues of videolink. Article 14(A) referring to the implementation of protective measures and an article that we discussed in our submission of the 28th in Article -- in paragraph 44. At the proposal of the investigating judge or the president of the Trial Chamber, the state prosecutor or the president of the court may require the interior affairs organs to take special measures to protect witnesses, and this is in Article 109, paragraph 3 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. I will not go any further. The standpoint of the OTP on a special law providing for the protection of witnesses is something that the Defence can comment on as follows: It is true that such a law is necessary, but the constitutional charter regulating the relations between the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, which deals with the status of the joint state of Serbia and Montenegro, contains the following provisions: The Law on Criminal Procedure valid in Montenegro, which is part of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro, regulates the issue of protection of witnesses in Articles 108 to 109, that is Articles 108 and 109 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Montenegro. The Republic of Montenegro has adopted a special law on witness protection in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Montenegro, number 65 of 2004, and this has been in force as of the 1st of April, 2005. This law on the protection of witnesses encompasses the conditions and procedures for providing protection for witnesses, a commission for the implementation of witness protection programmes, a unit for witness protection, the application and extension of the programme of protection, the kinds of protection, and so on and so forth. I will not go into this any further. The regulations from this law which I have just quoted are in accordance with Article 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY providing for witness protection measures. It is fully in harmony with this. To clarify to the Court, the Defence also states that the law on the criminal procedure of the Republic of Serbia in Article 220 regulates the issue of legal aid, which has been made more specific in Article 8, paragraph 1, of the law on the organisation of courts in the Republic of Serbia as the lex specialis. Article 220 on the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Serbia provides for all organs participating in criminal proceedings to provide the necessary assistance. The special Article 8 of the law on courts of the Republic of Serbia reads that courts are duty-bound to offer each other legal aid, and other state organs and organisations are duty-bound to provide the necessary aid and the necessary information to the courts. What does this mean in practice? In practice, this means that should a problem arise in the case of a witness from the Republic of Croatia who does not wish to testify in Serbia, such a witness by a decision of the Trial Chamber for war crimes of the court in Belgrade can be sent to testify before a court in Podgorica in Montenegro, and the testimony of this witness can then be treated as evidence in the criminal proceedings before the war crimes court in Serbia. This means that this witness can make his statement with the protection contained in the Law on Criminal Procedure of Montenegro. As for the Defence response to the positions of the Republic of Croatia, and I will speed up a little, the Croatian government considers that the proceedings should be conducted on the territory where the crime was perpetrated. Also, Croatia feels that it -- for reasons of expedience, this should be done and also that witnesses testifying before the courts in Serbia in the Ovcara case were intimidated. The Defence, however, wishes to point out that in the report of the NGO Foundation for Humanitarian Law in Belgrade, the director of which has been given authority or, rather, is protecting the rights of the victims of Ovcara before the court, in his report of the 6th of April, 2005, says as follow: "The proceedings before the war crimes court in Belgrade are conducted in a professional manner with a view to establishing the truth and the individual criminal responsibility of each accused and establishing the facts which might help to identify the victims." This report was signed by the regional team, which includes observers from Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, and independent observers. From this report, it follows that the impression they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you. The report, has that been submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order not to lose time, allow me to conclude with a few sentences and then I will tender this report and the three bills I have mentioned. I will submit this to the Court at the end of my address. I do have these both in English and in Serbian. It is incorrect that most of the evidence is on the territory of the Croatia, as the Croatian government claims. It is true that the material traces are there, that an on-site investigation has been conducted, forensic reports have been submitted, and the victims are from Croatia. However, most of the witnesses are in Serbia. And how the Defence will bring these witnesses before the court -- may I proceed? Thank you. As most of these witnesses will be military personnel who are now in Serbia and people who are members of various volunteer organisations as well as persons who are accused in the Ovcara case and large numbers of politicians in important positions as representatives of the local government in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, there is an objective danger that none of these witnesses will appear before the courts in Croatia. I wish to point out to Your Honours a recent case, and this is a case which is well known and refers to the arrest of Colonel Cedomir Brankovic. Cedomir Brankovic was arrested as a member of an official military delegation from Belgrade to Bulgaria. He is a colonel in the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, and there was an arrest warrant issued by the Croatian judiciary saying that he had participated in crimes around Novska in 1991. In the meantime, he has been released by the judiciary in Bulgaria. And I wish to conclude by saying that a fair trial cannot be conducted in Croatia because most defence witnesses will be from the group of people I have described. Your Honours, to conclude, as I have sufficient copies, I tender Article 21, paragraph 1, on the law on the application of the Statute of the ICTY [as interpreted]. I think that in the transcript -- I have an objection to the transcript. When I was discussing Article 21, I said "Article 21 of the law on the application of the Statute of the ICTY -- of the ICC," and the transcript reads "ICTY," and this is of crucial importance. Furthermore, I wish to tender as Exhibit number 2 the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Montenegro. As Exhibit 3, I tender Article 220 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Serbia and Article 8 on the law on the organisation of courts of the Republic of Serbia. And furthermore, I wish to tender the report of The Front For Humanitarian Law dated the 6th of April, 2005. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. One very factual question just for myself to see whether there will be any legal issue. You talked about witnesses who would not appear in Croatia, and you mentioned among them those accused in the Ovcara case at this moment. Are they -- are these accused in detention at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the accused in the Ovcara case are, of course, in detention except perhaps for one or two who are not in detention for health reasons. However, as accused before the court in Belgrade, they -- as themselves have said in war crimes proceedings where we as counsel were observers, they will not agree to testify as witnesses should be -- should the proceedings be conducted before a Croatian court in Croatia. I assume that perhaps there are indictments under seal in the Croatian judiciary for other crimes, and there are proceedings in absentia, so that I am quite sure of this. And what I mentioned, that is the case of Colonel Brankovic, this shows that large numbers of military personnel are not sure that they have not been indicted in indictments under seal by the Croatian judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're finished? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a technical problem here in view of the schedule we received. I know that a break is supposed to start soon, and my contribution should take about 15 minutes. It would be better for me to finish without the break if Your Honour agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you finish within 15 minutes, you're allowed to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, and all the parties to these proceedings, I will cover three topics that have not been covered, at least not in a detailed way in our written submissions. One concern has become the core discussion about the possible referral of this case to national jurisdiction, that is the focal point of the entire Article 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the concept over which all the swords of arguments of the parties are being crossed here, both in written submissions and in oral arguments. That is the concept of fair trial. And your decision, if you find that all the requirements from the Rule 11 bis C have been met, must be based on a firm conviction that the accused will have a fair trial. We have to discuss one aspect of a fair trial which follows from Article 10(2)(b) of the Statute, that is the presumption of innocence and that a trial has to be independent and impartial. The judiciary both in Serbia and Montenegro and in Croatia is formally independent of the executive and legislative authorities. Maybe the representatives of these authorities present here will not like our observations, but it is our obligation to act first and foremost in the interest of our clients and to try to provide for them within the remit of our powers the best conditions for a trial to be fair. One of the most important, if not the most important, principles of a fair trial is the presumption of innocence. It is the obligation of all state authorities not only to refrain from any statements regarding the outcome of the proceedings but also to influence the public opinion not to threaten this fundamental right of the accused. In the general comment number 13, paragraph 7, adopted by the Commission for Human Rights of the United Nations of the 15th of August, 1997, as an instruction for interpreting the international covenant on civil and political rights that has been adopted by both states represented in this courtroom stipulates as follows regarding the presumption of innocence: "The presumption of innocence implies the right of the accused to be treated in keeping with this principle." Therefore, all representatives of the authorities are duty-bound to refrain from pre-judging the outcome of the trial. The accused and their Defence counsel have just concern, just reason to -- to be concerned that a possible trial in Croatia could be affected interests by the vested interests of the executive authorities. It is obvious that the Ovcara case and a possible trial of our clients, who are frequently referred to as the "Vukovar troika," has considerable weight in the Croatian public opinion. The officials of the Croatian authorities have frequently given statements about the importance of this trial and their interest in having the case referred. This in itself is not perhaps a reason for our concern, but if such statements contain certain qualifications whereby the authorities show that they are interested not only in having their case referred but also in the outcome of the trial, then this is cause for deep concern of the Defence that the trial may not be independent or impartial. Some of this has been dealt with in our response to the motion of the Prosecution for the referral in paragraph 41. We now have to be precise. Specifically the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Croatia who also signed the submission before you stated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stated the ongoing proceedings for referral of this case, and this was broadcast in the news bulletin of the Croatian television of the 9th of February, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to slow down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to keep my promise to finish soon. I will repeat the quotation. "Since this is the gravest crime ever committed in Croatia, we will present all the necessary arguments for Croatia to receive this case." In the news bulletin of the same Croatian television broadcast on the 12th of March, 2005, the same Minister of Justice states as follows, I quote: "I believe it would be a very good thing if Croatia got the Vukovar troika, because that is where the greatest genocide after Srebrenica that was committed after the Second World War." Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia, Mrs. Jadranka Kosor made another statement published by Vjesnik on the 30th of March, 2005: "I personally believe that the Vukovar troika should be held accountable before the International Criminal Court, because we would not achieve anything by transferring this case to the Croatian judiciary, and anyway, the International Criminal Court stipulates the severest sentences for this." And finally, let us take a look at the submission of the Government of Croatia in this case, conclusion IV page 6, I will quote it in English: "After referral it will transfer the case to the competent courts for further proceeding and sentencing. "... croatian criminal law provides a suitable normative framework for prosecution and trial of the case." In other words, the Croatian government demands in its written submission to take over this case that the -- so that the accused should be tried and convicted before the competent Croatian court. A possible acquittal is never mentioned in this submission, only sentencing. Regarding the Ademi Norac case and the Croatian submission concerning this, which is also the subject of your decision, Your Honour, the Croatian submission never mentions the word "sentencing." It reads: "Croatian criminal law provides a suitable normative framework for Prosecution and trial of the case." Both submissions were signed on behalf of the Croatian government by the Minister of Justice whose statements I have just quoted. Maybe there are people who do not see any reason for concern regarding the independence of the judiciary in such political statements. However, according to these statements as expressions of the opinion of the highest representatives of the Croatian executive authorities, these accused are a priori considered as persons who are planned to be convicted and given the highest sentences. If we put all this in the context in which the Republic of Croatia has filed a case at the ICC here in The Hague against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro, for genocide, then we clearly see the vested interest of the executive powers in the outcome of these proceedings. One of the grounds for the charge of genocide are the events that are the subject of these proceedings. You can see that in paragraph 12 of the -- of the suit filed by Croatia against the FRY of the 2nd of July, 1999. We haven't prepared a copy but we can give you one after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This shows you how much time the interpreters need to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. translate what you say. May I take it when you refer to a case filed at the ICC that you are actually referring to the ICJ? International Court of Justice rather than the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. It is the ICJ. That is a case between states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will move on to another subject. That is the subject that we have covered in our response of the 1st of March, and our second submission dated the 28th of March, 2005. That is the issue of the right to chosen counsel. From what the representatives of the states have written, it follows unequivocally that the currently appointed counsel in this case could continue to represent the accused only before the judiciary of Serbia and Montenegro. As we already pointed out -- what we already pointed out in our first submission has been confirmed by the government of the Republic of Croatia in its submission, paragraph 4, page 5, namely the fact that before Croatian courts only Croatian citizens can act in the capacity of counsel. I probably don't need to particularly emphasise to what extent the relationship of trust and privilege between the accused and counsel is fundamental to the preparation of defence and to what extent it is a sine qua non of the right to chosen counsel. All the Defence counsel appointed here have been named because they meet the necessary requirements, have the necessary qualifications and have been chosen be by the accused themselves. Without wishing to give ourselves special importance, we do have to point out two important facts: In view of the time we have already spent working on this case, we are all of us ready for a trial to begin immediately, and the second fact is that all the Defence teams have already implemented a great number of contacts out of which a great number are contacts with confidential sources, sensitive sources. We provided a detailed explanation in para 63 of our first response to the motion of the Prosecutor. Our clients are fully convinced that the lawyer/client privilege could not exist with lawyers from Croatia because of the peculiarities of this case, at least not at a levelness for an adequate defence. This conclusion also follows from the prevailing public opinion in Croatia regarding this indictment, a public opinion that has existed for many years now, that concerns also the role of the JNA in the Vukovar events and concerning our clients themselves. Such an attitude, such a relationship, that is, the privileged client/lawyer relationship could not be established on the level of cooperation between counsel through the authorised Croatian law offices either. Such representation through mediators without direct involvement in the courtroom and without direct participation in the proceedings would considerably restrict professional conduct and would jeopardise the most important principles prescribed in the preamble of our professional Code of Conduct as Defence counsel before this Tribunal. In view of all our arguments already provided on this issue in our written submissions, the Defence believes that the principle of chosen counsel and adequate defence as one of the important segments of a fair trial in this specific case can be achieved fully only if the case is transferred to the judiciary of Serbia and Montenegro. And finally in our oral arguments we would like to touch upon one other subject, namely the problems regarding the application of the provisions from Rule 11 bis (D)(iv), which gives the Prosecution the possibility to send monitors to attend the trial before a national court as well as the possibility to replace the order for a referral and request deferral to the ICTY as envisaged by Rule 11 bis (F) of the Rules. We have already presented our views on this in our last submission, paragraph 65, 68. To a certain degree the vision of the Defence, the views of the Defence, are compatible with the position of the OTP as expressed in paragraph 31 of their latest submission. Still, the Defence believes that it is necessary to point to the Chamber to what extent this problem is important from the aspect of independence of the judiciary and the principle of a fair trial. In one of previous proceedings concerning the issue of referral - I believe it was in the Ademi Norac case - I heard the position of one of the participants in this discussion that the greatest guarantee that a trial would be fair is the fact that at every stage of the proceedings the Tribunal may request deferral again, which would have far reaching and negative consequences on the confidence of the international community in that national jurisdiction. Such an understanding can be only one side of the coin. The other side of the coin is the awareness of all those who would be taking an active part in the proceedings, I mean the Judges and the Prosecutors on behalf of the state concerned, the awareness that their conduct is not consistent with the requirements for a fair trial of somebody who is monitoring the trial. The highest standard for ensuring a fair trial wherever it is taking place must be the independence and impartiality of the trial. We all have to be aware of fact that the provision on the monitoring of a national trial and the possibility to request deferral of case back at any stage is a huge pressure on a national court. We have no reason to doubt that it is your purpose to contribute in any event under any circumstances to a conduct of the trial without any pressure at all. That is why we stated in our written submission that we are concerned by the solution provided by Rule 11 bis (F), namely that the Prosecution is authorised to initiate proprio motu a deferral to the ICTY. According to the Statute, the mandate of the Office of the Prosecutor is to prosecute -- is to prosecute. If we interpret this provision of Rule 11 bis (F), it follows that there is an expectation for the trial to be impartial and competent only in favour of the accused but not to his detriment. What if it turns out that the trial is partial to the detriment of the accused? Would the Prosecution even then request deferral? I am concluding now. In view of all these facts, we believe that is only the Tribunal, personified by this Trial Chamber, either the Trial Chamber or the Referral Chamber that must within its own authority ensure an objective monitoring of a national trial without exerting at any moment any pressure on an independent jurisdiction. Only then would the highest standards for a fair trial be accomplished, attained, and only would such a trial shed light on the truth. We will come to the truth and that is one of the mandates for -- with which this Tribunal has been established, that is to re-establish reconciliation among the nations of Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not at this moment at stake. I'd like to give -- Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems that I still owe a response to the OTP with respect to the witness I mentioned who was killed. utterances.text: Yes. It was, I do understand, just an assumption of yourself of a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was much need to have this, I again doubt that, but at least it's perfectly clear now. Mr. Ljajic, could I -- I'd like to give you an opportunity to make further submissions on behalf of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LJAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, allow me first of all to express my satisfaction that I am in a position to take part in these proceedings today on behalf of my country. These proceedings are of special importance to us, particularly in view of the fact that Serbia and Montenegro wish to completely fulfil their obligations towards the Tribunal in the process of facing the past and the process of reconciliation, and also in order for justice to be done. I also wish to thank the Office of the Prosecutor, because they did not bypass Serbia and Montenegro this time in their motion for referral. In the continuation of this discussion, the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro will acquaint the Chamber with the substantive and procedural requirements for referring this case to the judiciary of Serbia and Montenegro and provide answers to all the questions that might be asked in this respect. Let me point out several issues that will arise in today's discussion. Your Honours, one of the basic pre-conditions for a successful completion strategy of the Tribunal is to enable national judicial systems to try the accused for war crimes fairly, impartially, and expediently. In that respect, Rule 11 bis is not only a vehicle for relieving the Tribunal of a great number of cases, but it is also a means to test national judicial systems as well as to encourage and empower them to try war crimes and other crimes as well, not only those that are currently before the Tribunal. And finally, this is the best way for the public opinion to face the crimes that have been perpetrated and for that same public opinion to fully accept the decisions of courts already taken in trials. Serbia and Montenegro is firmly and unequivocally committed to having the greatest possible number of cases under indictments against citizens of Serbia and Montenegro to be referred to our courts, which have demonstrated that they are ready and willing to prosecute and try the accused in war crime cases respecting the highest international standards. I'm firmly convinced that the case against the accused Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic, should be referred to Serbia and Montenegro. There is many reasons in favour of such a decision and I will point out among them the principle of expediency and economical nature of proceedings. As we have pointed out several times here, the Special Chamber for War Crimes of the District Court in Belgrade is already conducting proceedings in the case of crimes on the Ovcara farm that has been started in cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and by merging these two cases we could save a considerable amount of time and financial resources without any prejudice to the accused. At the same time, we would achieve a unity of justice because all the persons accused of this crime would be tried in the same place, under the same criteria, and that in its turn would enable us to find out the full truth about this tragic event. I have to state on this occasion that referring this case to another court in another state would have considerable negative consequences. Namely, that could heighten the resistance in Serbia and Montenegro to cooperation with the Tribunal in The Hague. And I have also to point out that considerable progress has been achieved in the past period in terms of cooperation of Serbia and Montenegro with the Tribunal. Of course, I'm perfectly aware of the fact that cooperation with the Tribunal is an obligation and it cannot depend on the attitude of our public opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slow down a little bit, because the interpreters might have a difficult job following you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LJAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my last sentence, namely that I'm perfectly aware of the fact that our cooperation with the Tribunal cannot depend on the disposition of our public opinion or any other circumstances. It is primarily our moral, political, and legal obligation that I believe we will meet fully. However, one of the most important functions of the legal process is to do justice. Justice can be done only if it is seen to have been done in the public and if it is accepted as such, and that is why I believe the Tribunal, just as national courts, will take that into account. And finally, two of the three accused present here surrendered voluntarily in Serbia and Montenegro. When surrendering, they did not have in mind the possibility that they could be transferred to another state. From the submissions and contributions of Defence teams, we can see that at this moment, they do not resist the possibility of referring the case to Serbia and Montenegro, but they are against referral to Croatia. I am convinced that by referring this case to Serbia and Montenegro, we would see a considerable encouragement of the process of facing the past and reconciliation in the region. The cooperation of our state with the Tribunal, with the OSCE, has resulted in the initiation of a project whose purpose is to make the public face the past and the crimes that have been committed and in this way contribute and strengthen the process of reconciliation in the region. I believe that the referral of this case will also make a significant contribution in this respect. Allow me, Mr. President, to give the floor to Mr. Djeric who is a member of the delegation of Serbia and Montenegro, and he will present our views on some legal issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ljajic. Mr. Djeric, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, it's always an honour to appear again as counsel before the International Tribunal. I am aware of the pressing time concerns, and I will try to be brief. I will deal with three issues which in the opinion of Serbia and Montenegro deserve further explanation. The first issue is interpretation of Rule 11 bis. One of the most important questions before the Referral Bench is how Rule 11 bis should be interpreted when two or more states are interested and willing to try the case. Rule 11 bis provides that it may be referred first to the state on whose territory the crime was committed; second, to the state in wit accused was arrested; or, third, to the state having jurisdiction and being willing and able to accept such a case. According to the Prosecution, these criteria should be ranked in a descending order of importance. However, we submit that there is nothing in Rule 11 bis that would lend support to such a conclusion. On the contrary. The use of the word "or" after each of the criteria set forth in the Rule indicates that they are of equal importance. According to Croatia, and I'm quoting their submission of 27 April at page 5, "International criminal law and customs prefer that proceedings are conducted by the court on whose territory the offence was committed." However, Croatia fails to provide any evidence for this conclusion, any evidence of international custom that would prefer that proceedings are conducted by the court on whose territory the offence was committed. We submit that there is no such rule in international law. For example, former president of this Tribunal, Judge Cassese in his treatise on international criminal law does not indicate any hierarchy on the basis of jurisdiction for international crimes, and I quote: "Traditionally states bring alleged perpetrators of international crimes to trial before their courts on the basis of one of three principles territoriality, passive nationality, the victim is a national of the prosecuting state; or active nationality, the perpetrator is national of the prosecuting state." Furthermore, he adds: "Recently the universality principle has emerged." This is in Professor Cassese international criminal law at page 277. "Therefore, we submit that the three criteria in Rule 11 bis are of equal importance. The fulfillment of any of these criteria is the objective precondition or the second step under Rule 11 bis, and it is this second step which involves an assessment by the Bench of whether the accused will receive a fair trial and that the death penalty will not be imposed or carried out." We submit that these are the two fundamental considerations that should govern the decision of the Bench under Rule 11 bis. And as we explained in our written submission, these are the only two express requirements under Rule 11 bis once this jurisdictional basis requirement is fulfilled. Consequently, if and only if the Bench deems that these two requirements, fair trial and the prohibition of the death penalty, are equally fulfilled by the states concerned, it should take into account other considerations such as the principle that justice should be rendered as closely to the victims as possible, the expediency of the trial, the availability of evidence, et cetera, et cetera. Now, in this context of these two express requirements of Rule 11 bis, we wish to point out that there have been some reservations as to whether the accused in the present case could receive a fair trial in Croatia. These reservations are based on the reports made by the OSCE mission in Croatia. It is submitted that the Bench should give utmost consideration to these reports because they are directly related to the fundamental criterion under Rule 11 bis and that is the fair trial. Furthermore, these reports have been made by an impartial international monitoring body and this obviously adds a lot to their credibility. In this regard, I would like to draw the attention of the Bench to the recent presentation by Ambassador Semneby, head of the OSCE mission in Croatia, made to the OSCE permanent council, which is the highest body in the OSCE, on 10 March 2005. This presentation was made after the Prosecution's submission of 8 February this year which contained other OSCE statements in its annex 3. And I will have a copy of this statement from Ambassador Semneby for the Bench and the parties later. Now, in the presentation Ambassador Semneby said that ethnic bias existed in lower court trials in Croatia and concluded that the mission's monitoring of war crimes issues was likely to continue, and I quote: "As long as there are significant problems related to bias against Serb defendants in lower courts and conversely laxity towards Croatian indictees." End of quote. Your Honours, with your permission I would now move to the second issue. The accused are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro and were nationals of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At the time of their transfer or surrender, it was prohibited to extradite Yugoslav nationals under the constitution. It was only possible to transfer Yugoslav nationals for a trial before an international court or tribunal. Now, if the transfer of the accused to the International Tribunal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would only be a first step towards their transfer to a third state, a first step on their trip to the third state, we submit this would amount to extradition. This would ex post facto put the government of Serbia and Montenegro in a very uncomfortable situation and would amount to a breach of confidence. The government acted pursuant to Article 29 of the Statute. Article 29 is an exception in a rule that states have a first call to prosecute persons within their jurisdiction that are accused of international crimes. This exception should be interpreted narrowly and cannot reasonably encompass the authority of the International Tribunal to perform what would amount to a two-step extradition. Therefore, we submit the state which transferred or surrendered the accused should be given preference to prosecute if it's willing and able to do so and if it fulfils the requirements of Rule 11 bis. Further, it is important to note the provisions of the European Convention on extradition. Both Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro as well as all other states of the former Yugoslavia are parties to the convention. Article 6 of the convention recognises the right of states to refuse extradition of their own nationals, and this also shows that Article 29 of the Statute should be interpreted narrowly. In all other situations not covered by Article 29, states may refuse the transfer of their own nationals for trial in other states. Furthermore, both Croatia and Serbia made declarations under the European Convention on Extradition. In these declarations they asserted their right to refuse to extradite their own nationals. None of them objected to others' declaration. It is submitted that this way, a reciprocal obligation was constituted between Croatia on the one side and Serbia and Montenegro on the other, the obligation not to request extradition of each other's nationals in cases where their state of nationality opposes such a request. I will recall that the accused in the present case are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro. Finally, I would refer to Article 15 of the European Convention on Extradition. This article allows extradition to a third state only with the consent of the original surrendering state. This is also evidence of the firm position of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, and other states of the former Yugoslavia that re-extradition is not allowed without the consent of the original surrendering state. It is submitted to the Bench that this practice, an opinion juris should be taken into account by the Bench when it considers the request of Croatia in the present case. Finally, Your Honours, I would conclude but by just pointing out that annex 3 of our submission of 28th April, contains all the relevant provisions in our domestic law on the witness protection. It, in our opinion, presents a more comprehensive outlook of this issue than the one presented by the Defence and the Prosecution in their written submissions. This will conclude my presentation, Your Honours, and we stand at your disposal for any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djeric. I'd like to give an opportunity now, Mr. Horvatic, to you to make any further submissions on behalf of Croatia.
