utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: The old professor always forgets something, but I do hope I will not forget what is the main point in my explanation. It is my great honour to be the second time here in this room with almost the same colleagues and with the same Chamber, of course. When we received the invitation for this hearing carefully listing what is our position and now because of the majority of the participants in this hearing, I will continue in Croatian language. [Interpretation] The government of the Republic of Croatia has been invited to attend this hearing and, if it wishes, to orally present additional arguments to the submission dated the 27th of April of this year. My intention was to clarify certain details, but the course of these proceedings has led me to conclude that it would be much more useful and acceptable to the Chamber were I to refer directly to what has been said here in relation to the standpoints of the government of the Republic of Croatia. My fundamental approach, which seems to me to be correct, is to focus on the legal issues at stake here and to exclude as far as is possible other issues which are not primarily legal but can, under certain circumstances, possibly affect a decision which is primarily a legal decision. I will begin with the legal issues on which the Prosecutor focused, and the Prosecution has a good understanding of what the main legal issues are. At the outset, the Prosecution stated, "We wish to be sure that the standpoints of the OTP will be taken into account in the judiciary to which the case will be referred." This applies primarily to the comment that unlike the case being tried in Belgrade, which does not include command responsibility, and command responsibility is one of the main issues. So the question is, will the applicable law be comparable to the applicable law at this Tribunal? The second issue is the ability of the state or, rather, the courts of the state to which the case is referred to conduct the proceedings. Thirdly, the cooperation between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro, the cooperation between the two states in criminal proceedings and how this will be manifested in this particular case. And the fourth issue that was raised was that of witnesses in Belgrade, discrepancies in the number of testimonies before the trial of the 17 accused in Belgrade. With respect to the first issue, in the Ademi and Norac case on the 17th of February, 2005, before this Trial Chamber, we presented material in which we attempted to respond fully to all the legal issues raised in connection with the applicable law, with command responsibility, and especially command responsibility as the foundation for responsibility in specific cases during the time that both these cases originated or, rather, the time that the events took place. This is all available to the Chamber, so I will not repeat it here. By force of law and the international sources of law which are part of the Croatian legal system, the court would be duty-bound to apply those legal provisions. With respect to the ability to conduct the proceedings, I must say quite sincerely that from public opinion and the reports of non-government organisations to certain individual cases which were commented upon while they were still in the first instance or trial stage, there were very many misconceptions about whether a certain judiciary was competent, able to conduct the proceedings or not. I will use a metaphor here, a comparison, and I will say that the situation in Serbia and Montenegro and in Croatia, in both these states, the situation today is different from what it was some time ago or perhaps a decade ago. As for the witnesses who testified in the case of the 17 in Belgrade, I will not go into this because it is a complex issue to which I will refer when I speak about whether witnesses from one state dare go to another state to testify, whether the victims and witnesses and their relatives wish to testify or can testify and so on. The Defence in its standpoints expressed on behalf of Mrksic and Radic stated expressly in response to a question by Judge Orie that these were voluntary surrenders and they mentioned Rule 11 bis, which speaks of cases of referral to the authorities of a country in which the accused was arrested. The brilliant interpretation by two attorneys that I have heard here, as well as by the representative of Serbia and Montenegro of the relation of surrender, extradition, and re-extradition can be of great interest for the legal literature. However, in this case, only Rule 11 bis applies. The government of the Republic of Croatia submits that this has no correlation with extradition and re-extradition as mentioned here and even the documents of the council of Europe. As for two or three arguments referring to the three possibilities, I will speak in English now. [In English] "The territory the crime was committed or in which the accused was arrested or having jurisdiction and being willing and adequately prepared to accept such a case," [Interpretation] In our view, these three cases are not of equal standing. I think the representative of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro overlooked something, and I esteem the gentleman in question, that were the case referred to a third country having jurisdiction and being willing and adequately prepared, this is only one of two solutions where according to the principles of international law and customary law absolute priority is to be given to the state and criminal justice system in whose territory the crime was committed. We can discuss whether 11 bis put these three cases on the same level or not, but if Croatia is asked to prove that (A)(i) has priority, we can point to the Statute of The Hague Tribunal, and we feel that this is a well-known fact which needs no proof. Even the penal code of the former Yugoslavia to which we were subjected until 1990 and the new Yugoslav law of 1993 and the new penal code of Serbia and Montenegro, as well as the new Croatian code puts the territorial principle first. The other considerations and principles are all subsidiary when it comes to competence and the application of law. I will not touch upon the cases mentioned by the Defence and the attempts made to link these with confidence in the Croatian judiciary. Whether a witness was killed or died a natural death is something we could discuss in a separate hearing, but I do not feel the need to counter this argument, because it is not something that supports the claim that the Croatian judiciary is not able to conduct the proceedings. As for one of the important aspects of the judiciary and its ability to conduct the trial, that is witness protection, the situation presented by the Defence was not quite clear to me. They compared the laws of the Republic of Montenegro and the laws of the Republic of Serbia. In one of these states, witness protection is provided, and in the other, international assistance between these two countries is provided for. I feel that this is something that complicates matters and obscures the clarity and transparency of the legal proceedings in this or any other trial referred to Serbia and Montenegro. It seems to me that the coherence of criminal law and the other elements of the legal system in that country are not sufficiently guaranteed as is the coherence of the legal system in the Republic of Croatia. It seems to me that in this situation, the arguments put forward to challenge the suitability or the ability of the Croatian judiciary are simply at the level of speculation. The Defence stated that the accused before the Belgrade court, as far as the Defence are aware, will not appear as witnesses in Croatia because they suspect that there are secret indictments against them in Croatia. This assumption is not of a legal nature, neither is the assumption that the Croatian judiciary will judge according to statements made by the government. In Croatia, there is a division of powers between the judiciary, the executive, and the legislative branches. People can express different opinions, not only in Serbia and Montenegro or Croatia, but also in France, the USA, or any country in this world. When the president of a large federal state states on one occasion, "We will condemn this severely," and he was speaking about a military crime, nobody doubted that the judiciary would be impartial. The same goes for statements made by the Ministry of Justice and the Deputy Minister Jadranka Kosor which were cited on Croatian television. This can only show that the Croatian government wants the territorial principle to be applied in the Croatian judiciary and that the courts will have the competence they have under the constitution. And should the Minister of Justice or the Deputy Prime Minister really during the trial, or whether even if the statements already made were considered to be attempts to influence the court, they would be held criminally responsible for attempting to influence the court. This interpretation also applies to a rather skilful discussion of the difference between the words trial and sentence. In the Ademi Norac case it was said that a trial would be held, and in this case the Croatian state is quoted to have said, "[In English] "After referral it will transfer the case to the competent courts for further proceedings and sentencing." [Interpretation] My poor knowledge of English asks me to conclude that whoever wrote this, and it was not me, that when they said "sentencing," what they meant was "to hand down a judgement." If and when this Honourable Chamber decided to refer the case to the Croatian judiciary based on legal interpretations of Rule 11 bis and the competency of the Croatian judiciary, I wish to assure you, not only the Chamber but also the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro and the Defence, that there will be cooperation not only between the two states in this case on the basis of the convention of the Council of Europe and on the basis of what our consciences ask of us but also on the basis of our cooperation in other cases, which was demonstrated when there was a videolink recently between the county court in Zagreb and the District Court in Belgrade, which were in direct communication. This also, of course, supports the argument that there would be such cooperation were the case to be referred to Serbia and Montenegro. And to conclude this part of my presentation, and I am willing to answer any questions, I must say that the claims made about the trust in the counsel that would be chosen, because foreign nationals cannot appear as Defence counsel in the Republic of Croatia, it has been shown in many cases that the chosen Defence counsel was a national of the Republic of Croatia, but he was able to have co-counsel even in the courtroom who were attorneys in other countries, and their only limitation was that they could not address the Chamber directly but they could assist in the defence. This is what any counsel in Croatia would do, and this is also what counsel in Serbia and Montenegro do when they are acting as Defence counsel for Croatian nationals, and this is the principle that is applied, and professionally we feel there is no doubt that this would be the case. What leads to uncertainty and mistrust are the political aspects, which of course must be taken into account. But the extent to which such political considerations can be allowed to oppose or influence the legal considerations is up to you to decide, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Horvatic. The Chamber highly appreciates that the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro and Croatia have focused on the most important parts and both limited themselves to less than 25 minutes where 30 minutes was scheduled. One question for you, Mr. Horvatic, at this very moment, a very factual question, could you give us any information about plans that were mentioned by one of the Defence counsel of trying, as he said, the Vukovar troika before a local court in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many questions are here, and I -- I leave it for your question and direct answer. There are many indictment in Croatia from 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, and many trials in absence. As I know, there are one indictment against these three gentlemen sitting here. But anyhow, any communication between the public prosecutor from Vukovar and from the president of the court of Vukovar, I have no evidence that this communication was and this conversation was here, but let us say if it was two or three weeks ago, that was only communication unofficial, and the official is statement by the general prosecutor any case, if it is in trial here, in any stage of procedure is immediately stopped with any -- in spite of the fact that we have some evidence if the Prosecutor from The Hague ask for the -- any documents and evidence. So there is no any trial, no any procedure there official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that I'm quite clear. And there is some -- in addition, there are some possibility that one possible witness is also one of the person who is in absence is condemned. That is possibility. But in such a case, it will be our obligation to obey the rule of the international law, and if the witness is coming to Croatia or his statement or has statement, it will be by link --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just asking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the three persons, Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Radic, and Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will not extend my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could ask a further question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I will give you an opportunity to address the Chamber, but first Mr. Parker would have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Judge Parker, Your Honour, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, what court in Croatia would try this case if it were to be referred to Croatia? Is that an exclusive jurisdiction or is it possible that this case could be referred, for example, to a court in Vukovar? Could that be clarified, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes. The clarification is there was some opinion in our public opinion that if the case would be transferred, referred to Croatia, the competent court would be Vukovar. No way. The only court, it will be Zagreb. The only one. There are four courts for the trial. We explained that in the previous cases, Zagreb, Rijeka, Osijek, and Split. In this case it will be Zagreb. That will be decision of the Ministry of Justice in accordance with the president of Supreme Court. There is no any possibility to come to Vukovar because of the law, existing law which not shall be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, and I apologise that I interrupted ahead of what had earlier been an indication of counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give Mr. Djeric an opportunity to add, because it seems that he would like to add something, I'd first address Defence counsel. Mr. Horvatic just referred to the Ademi Norac materials submitted by the Croatian government. I take that it's sufficiently clear to counsel that whatever submissions were made with a -- of a general character as to the law and the competence of organs, the legal structure in Croatia that this Chamber will take that into consideration as well, that reference can be made to it, and that counsel are aware of that and have had an opportunity to look at that material. Since I do not see any vehement objections, I take it that my assumption is right. Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps I'm pre-empting some of your questions, but I -- we think that we are here to assist the Court, so I would just briefly outline a couple of points that perhaps need to be outlined. We understand this is not a contest and we are here to assist the Court. Therefore, I will say just a couple of sentences on superior responsibility. This issue was extensively discussed in Norac case, and in Mejakic case where Serbia and Montenegro was represented was discussed to some extent. It was -- I look at the transcript. I was not here at the time. It was not really thoroughly discussed, but for the sake of the efficiency of the present proceedings, I can say that the analysis of the amicus curiae in Norac of Professor Damaska Krapac is in our opinion fully applicable to the law which in -- which before the courts of Serbia and Montenegro would be applicable in the present case. Now, in essence both in Croatia and in Serbia and Montenegro, the same provisions will apply, and this is in essence the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was then adopted as Croatian law some -- at some point mid-1991. It continued to be under the same name -- our Criminal Code had some amendments in our case related to the sentence which was now in 1993 the sentence was only 20 years, but otherwise the concepts, the provisions, the analysis provided by Professor Damaska Krapac and especially very helpful discussions by Professor Krapac in this tribunal are fully applicable to the present case. Of course, should you wish to go into any of the details of superior responsibility, we can -- we are able to assist you. But I can say that for the sake of the economy of the proceedings, the same analysis applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the legal basis is exactly the same. It's your common legal origin. If, of course, there would be any case law developed after you separated, then of course the Chamber would very much like to know. But if there is none, then of course could accept that it's the analysis of the legal texts that is valid not only for Croatia but also for Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm not aware of any cases that would be relevant to the issue of superior responsibility or to the concepts that are related to this -- to this concept of international law. I could only say that with respect to Ovcara case before the Belgrade court, there we have a trial of persons accused to be hands-on perpetrators, and I don't think that with respect to most of these persons the concept of superior responsibility would apply at all. It is true, as my learned colleague from Croatia said, there is no issue of superior responsibility before the -- before the Belgrade court, but there are [inaudible] perpetrators. Now, if I may just say a couple of more sentences on 11 bis, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you -- because I have many questions also for counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I will be very brief. I would just say, first, that my colleagues and myself looked at the Statute of the ICTY, and we don't see any provision which could be related to the -- to the issue of 11 bis, and that is, what is the international basis of jurisdiction in situations of international crimes? There is no territoriality principle in the statute of the Tribunal except for the fact that it is territorial -- territorially it has the jurisdiction over the territory of former Yugoslavia. That is the only thing. Now, my learned colleague said that it's traditional concept that territorial jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of the place where the crime was committed is the primary source and primary criterion on jurisdiction, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I would submit that this is indeed the case but within internal domestic legal orders. It is true that the place where the crime was committed should be the source of jurisdiction in the first place. However, and as I demonstrated by quoting Professor Krapac, in international law you don't see a hierarchy. In international practice, I am not aware of the hierarchy between territorial jurisdiction and other forms of jurisdiction. Finally, I really don't see in words of article -- of Rule 11 bis any distinction between the three criteria. As for the question of whether political considerations should be taken into account in this trial, this proceeding, I completely agree that this -- that we have legal issues in front of ourself. However, the requirement of fair trial in order to be given substance in the current proceedings needs to take into account the facts which can be political facts, and one of the facts is the danger for witnesses. Another of the facts is that there are, according to our information, over 1.000, probably to 2.000 secret indictments which were not published in Croatia against persons of Serb origin who are, most of them, located on the territory of former -- of Serbia and who could -- some of them could be witnesses in the present case. Finally, I may say just one sentence on the issue of arrests and voluntary surrender. I think that this is important for the Chamber. We submit that 11 bis does not make a distinction between universal jurisdiction, territorial jurisdiction, and the place where the accused was arrested. That's the first point. Second point is that if you follow the express wording of 11 bis, you would -- one would say that, all right, an indictee who was arrested can be returned for trial in the state where he was arrested, but that would put a person who was arrested and who did not in a substance respect this court and come for a trial by himself. That would put the person who was arrested in a better position than the person who surrendered voluntarily to the court. And I don't think that judicial -- that propriety -- that this would be proper, not only considering the cooperation but considering the principle that one situation shows respect for the court, another situation which shows a natural reaction of the accused not to surrender or should not be the same as the situation as in which the accused surrendered. This is -- with this I conclude. Thank you very much and sorry for taking your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question directly related to your last observation. That's the following: If a French citizen voluntary goes to a Spanish court because he is indicted there, instead of waiting to be extradited, would that person who voluntary surrendered not also be in a disadvantageous position? Is that not true whenever someone voluntarily try surrenders to a foreign court and does not wait for -- to be extradited?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: My answer will be short. You will have to take into account a third state, a French citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm talking now about re-extradition by Spain to, for example, Italy. Isn't it true that the person who voluntarily surrendered to Spain, this French citizen, would be subject to extradition to Italy whereas the one who did not voluntarily surrender to Spain but was extradited is protected by the rule of speciality? Isn't that not a general situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, I can concur that it is, but in the situation of cooperation with the Tribunal, you have another -- another situation in the sense that you have a pressure to surrender or a pressure on the state to have one person arrested. And the second issue is that Article 29 is an exception. And Article 29 speaks about transfer and surrender and makes, really carves an enormous exception in the traditional, customary normal international law. And I see your point, but I think that this is a completely different situation. It is not a simple extradition situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course. But I mean the rules of extradition, re-extradition were invoked so that is the context in which we deal at the moment with the matter. I know, Professor Horvatic, you would like to. Could I give you two minutes and then because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Only one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only one minute. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: So I will not be involved in this -- such a nice discussion of extradition and re-extradition. My answer to your question is completely clear, that is not if you have something like that without this addition but colleague knows international and domestic criminal law maybe better than I, but only what I must say it is again one unacceptable statement from the representative of Serbia and Croatia -- and Montenegro that there is information of 1.000 or 2.000 secret indictment. Please be so kind and exclude that from your expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Information is not for nothing -- discussion in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers, you have been very brief in the beginning, and I'm not inviting you to take a lot of time, but of course you were very brief and did not expand on many subjects. If there would be any need at this moment to further expand on one of the issues that was raised, then I would like to give you an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very much appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would say "well, we have many questions perhaps I could ask" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I ask the representatives to switch off your microphones when you're not speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I missed the last comment that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I said if you would say there are some questions by the Bench that might already -- well, that might cover the subjects you'd like to address and therefore you'd prefer to wait, then we would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Bench raised a point that perhaps could cut down some of the areas of inquiry. The reason extradition has been raise the at all because it was framed in a response. We fully concur with Professor Horvatic that extradition is in no way implicated in this 11 bis proceeding, and if you will allow me perhaps it might assist any further discussion on it. 11 bis, like much of the provisions putting in place the Tribunal is a very specialised proceeding. Our position which I think is borne out eminently clearly in the Security Council mandates is that this is the other end of the spectrum. There is the Croatian getting primacy, always recognising concurrent jurisdiction, but giving primacy for conduct which is and should be in civilised nations universally condemned. The accused has no right in this instance to determine the forum in which that conduct which is to be condemned will be held when it comes through this Tribunal which has primacy. The first end of the spectrum is, if there is something out there that we have a reason under Article 9 to reel in, deferral. The referral is clearly the other end of the spectrum. It is fully a part of the obligation on all nations to assist in completion of the work of this Tribunal which from its inception was always ad hoc. Other nations who have contemplated bringing any actions have known effectively from day one that there would come a day where legal systems and financing, political will and maturity will have to merge and be ready to accept that which cannot be done by an ad hoc Tribunal which by definition does not have an infinite lifespan. Accordingly, I would ask that the Chamber simply, as I believe we are in agreement, accept that any concept of extradition is a red herring taking away the more important issues about what fairness procedural matters in place in the various courts that -- the various jurisdictions that seek now to take these cases. We of course don't need to remind the Chamber but just for the record that this case was confirmed in 1995 and the first accused only appeared before this Tribunal in 2002, the other two, 2003. So there was no apparent rush to set anything up. Referral or deferral of course has been invoked in some occasions -- on some occasions by the Office of the Prosecutor and the Tribunal. Again, there has been no evident rush by a number of states that could have jumped in recognising the need to try or bring these cases to justice to do so, and I think that that might assist in neutralising some of the apparent overbearing arguments on the extradition issue. I'll just try to finalise it. I think -- there maybe some things that are raised in your questions, Your Honour, that could cut short anything I have to say. One second, please, if I may. If I may, then, I would just defer to the Chamber's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I ask one thing, Ms. Somers. Although Mr. Djeric didn't touch upon the issue but Serbia and Montenegro in its written submission raised the issue related to the ICC rules in paragraph 52, I guess it is Rule 185, if you had the chance to ponder upon that issue, if you could elaborate on the similarities and dissimilarities with this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, I would ask first of all just to consider the difference in the ICC and we are a Security Council organ creation, that is a treaty creation. So if that has any bearing, that may be of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you refer to the principle of complementarity there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, the only thing that we would accept there is in common with the concept of extradition is the fact that it, like 11 bis, deals with a change of forum, and really that is where the likeness stops given the very special nature of the -- the reasons for its implementation -- I'm sorry, for its actual drafting as an implementation of a Security Council mandate to effect a completion date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would like to ask a further question of the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro concerning the case which was mentioned which is under way in -- already related in facts to the present case. I'm wanting assistance to learn how far that case has progressed. In view of the suggestion made in submission that if this case were referred, it might be possible to merge this case with that one. Is that still a legal and practical possibility? I leave it to the representatives to determine who might most easily reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. According it our information, the case is tried before the Belgrade court, Belgrade District Court. What -- according to our information, it is somewhere in the middle, to put it roughly, of the proceedings. Our prosecutor will have two possibilities. He will either try this -- if the case is referred, he would either try this case as a separate case, but he would be able to use all the experience, evidence, from the other case. And the -- another option is to merge the cases. But according to our information, this case has now been in progress for about a year before the court. However, if you take -- if you say one year, it's not one year of continuous trial. It was about 44 days of trial within this calendar year, but hopefully this will improve. The reason for such a small number of days of trial was that there were other trials for organised crime which are conducted in the same building. However, most probably we expect that the pace of the trial will improve in the future. I don't know whether that sufficiently answers your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a legal and a practical, feasible idea that there could be a merging of the two trials when the trial under way already in the District Court has progressed, as you say, to something like the middle stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I think that -- that it's quite a likely idea that case -- that the cases could be merged. They can be merged until the end of the main hearing of the currently going case before the Belgrade District Court. So until the hearings are concluded, the case is -- this case and the other case can be merged. And I -- from what we know from the -- from the people in special prosecutor's office and special court, their idea is to merge the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few very technical questions for Defence counsel. Mr. Borovic, you, and not you alone, paid a lot of attention to the absence of safe conduct. Witnesses would not go to Croatia, afraid of being arrested. Whether these are secret indictments or not, I'm not -- why would you not accept on the basis of the European Convention on the mutual assistance in criminal matters to which both Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro are a party and which provides clearly for a safe conduct, why would you expect just on the basis of absence in Croatian domestic law, why would you expect that Croatia would not fulfil its treaty obligations under that treaty which clearly provides for safe conduct for witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I deliberately quoted examples that deal with violations of the rights of the accused, especially when Defence witnesses are to testify before Croatian courts. First of all, I would like to respond to the question raised by the Croatian representative. He wanted the Defence counsel to state their views on this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, I would like to have an answer to my question. My question is simply you state that there is no safe conduct for witnesses, and I point to a clear provision which provides for a safe conduct in a treaty binding Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro, and I'd like to know why you do not accept that the legal framework for a safe conduct exists. If you say I've overlooked it, then that's also a clear answer, then. We're at least one step further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I did not overlook the existence of that convention, and I know that the parties are required to adhere to it, but I deliberately quoted examples such as the Lever case of which the OTP is very well-informed, and I raised a hypothesis of a case in which witnesses before a Croatian court could come to Croatia to testify without being afraid of revenge by the Croatian military. The report that I have in front of me deals with the broadcast of the Croatian television which says verbatim, "Investigating judge declared that Lever's death was a violent one." Another thing that is important for this Chamber in a series of reports that I will present to the Chamber is the report that says that he was one of the key witnesses for the ICTY. He asked for protection in Croatia, but he never received that protection. On the other hand, I quoted an example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're mixing up witness protection and safe conduct, which is not the same. I was asking about the legal framework for safe conduct, and of course witness protection is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the legal framework of course exists, and this European Convention signed by these two states is certainly something to be implemented. However, the justice system of Croatia has not been implementing it adequately so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question to you is the following: You said that the accused in the Ovcara case that are at trial at this moment in Belgrade would not consent to appear as witnesses in the -- if the case would be referred to Croatia. Does that same convention that I just quoted not provide for temporarily making available a witness who is detained and to keep him in detention during that short period of time in the state that would like to hear his testimony? And to that extent, would it not be a violation of the treaty obligations by Serbia and Montenegro if they would not send one of these detained accused if they are needed as witnesses in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we spoke primarily about the principle of a fair trial, and it was my position as Defence counsel that all the accused in the Ovcara case could do what you just explained quite rightly, but none of those accused would agree to testify. They would refuse to testify, and the Croatian justice system does not have any mechanisms to force such a witness to testify. So these two cases would be deprived of such evidence. The problem lies not in Serbia and Montenegro. Serbia and Montenegro will honour its obligation to deliver these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just imagine you're Defence counsel in a Croatian case, let's just for argument's sake assume against Mr. Mrksic, Radic, and Mr. Sljivancanin. You want to call a witness who is an accused in the Belgrade case. You address the court. The court asks for cooperation by Serbia and Montenegro by transferring on a temporary basis one of the accused in Belgrade to Croatia in order to testify. Why -- I mean, if they would not consent to that, these accused, could they not be sent and made available to the Croatian court by Serbia and Montenegro? Would that not be included in the treaty provisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia and Montenegro would do what the treaty requires them. But on the assumption that I appear as Defence counsel of one of those accused, we heard from the mouth of the Croatian representatives that I would not be allowed to ask one single direct question in favour of my clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... other Defence counsel. I hope you understood that I did not want to introduce that problem when discussing this one. I have one very short question before we have a break and it's the following: Many references are made to the OSCE report, the recent OSCE report, I should say. There are more. You referred to what you called a report and which I understand to be a press release of two pages where the OSCE reports are well documented. Is there any more substantive report or is it just this press release that you wanted to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a report dated 26th of April, 2005. It is literally a report on 50 pages, and I quoted from pages 20, 23, 27. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you provided to the Court is a press release from the Internet dated the 11th of May. So if you really want us to look at the report, because I do not see any 50-page report, then you should submit it. Before we have further questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may. If you allow me. We are not talking about a completely different report. This is a report by an NGO called Human Rights Foundation on 52 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't give it to us, if you just quote from reports and then when we cannot verify what is in that report, and that is why I asked whether you would submit that report, then of course the Chamber is not in a position to properly look at it. Yes? So if you want us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I will submit it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was an area that your questioning did not go into, and just for the sake of brevity, it is addressed in our submissions that applied to this afternoon's hearing in more detail. But in fact, we disagree with our learned colleagues that there is not an order to things. We believe that the international -- that the established norms do put locus of the crimes -- the commission of the crimes as first. There may be because of contemporary changes in policy with universal jurisdiction coming into the picture, a trend toward changing. But that does not negative -- negate the fact that there is a schema in the law that is recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you mind to copy the relevant parts of your submissions of the -- submissions relating to the afternoon hearing and provide it to Defence counsel during the break. Would that be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe they should have received it. If they hadn't they would have -- perhaps not. You're absolutely right, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 20 minutes, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After consultation, we'll start twenty minutes from now on this clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minor question to Mr. Vasic, a clarification. Serbia and Montenegro in its submission said that all of the accused are nationals of Serbia and Montenegro, and Mr. Djeric confirmed that in oral hearing. However, the record as to the nationality of Mr. Mrksic, it is not clear to me. My understanding is that he's born in Croatia, and he was a member of RSK. So could you clarify the nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Mr. Mrksic was indeed born in Croatia but at a time when Croatia was part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He does not have Croatian citizenship. The only citizenship that he has is that of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is currently Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A question I have relates to the law that would be applied were the case to be referred to Croatia, so I shall turn to Professor Horvatic. Much of your submissions tended to refer back to submissions made in the earlier case of Ademi and Norac. That, though, was an indictment of -- for offences in 1993, after there had been enacted in Croatia a new code, a Criminal Code, in 1993. The present offences are 1991. Does that affect any of the submissions that were advanced in Ademi, Norac, especially in the area of command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Honourable Judge, as you not remember, I can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. understand. I remember what I said on the last hearing, that it is for me very interesting situation that everybody's agree of something. Public prosecutor, Defence, and amicus curiae and me. That was the case of the law. Now is the same situation, because the law in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994 was the same in Croatia, in Serbia and Montenegro, and in Yugoslavia as called -- I don't know the final -- the final date of the Yugoslavia and starting with Serbia and Montenegro, but the same court was. Referring to the general part and referring to the criminal offences which is involved in this case, the same. We accept in 1990, 1991, we accept the same code, Yugoslav Criminal Code, with the same text only to change the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the Republic of Croatia, and with self-government government system was the democratic system of Croatia, nothing else. The main or all text of the code was the same, in the Serbia and Montenegro, in Yugoslavia and in Croatia, until 1st October, 1988 [sic]. Now we have our own Criminal Code. But it's applied, in all cases it's applied. This Criminal Code what was this time only if it is -- the new Criminal Code is in favour of accused person it will be applied as we explained in Ademi, Norac. As I see the situation the same code would be applied in Serbia and Montenegro if the case would be referred to this Tribunal and its -- in Zagreb Tribunal, the same -- the same text of code, Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you something further. I may have quite misunderstood the position. I thought that there was enacted in 1993 a new Criminal Code for Croatia. Not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. In 1993 was maybe some amendment in special part, but in this part, general part, and in this part which refers to the crimes against international community for humanitarian law. That was the same, untouchable, until 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that's when you encountered a new law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes we cancelled the -- the capital punishment immediately after our constitution which I have been informed it was two or three years later, but it not refers for this case because the capital punishment shall not apply according to another rule. But it is the same law. Maybe I'm wrong because of the same point of the representative of Republic of Serbia and Montenegro, but I think that it is the same law. I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we go back to the 1977 SFRY code as providing the text. You adopted it as Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But it is the same text until 1998 when you changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Let us repeat myself. In 1991, we accept the Yugoslav Criminal Code as a criminal code of Croatia, general part and special part, as it was before, 20 years before, from 1977. And we applied this code till 1998. And in 1998, it's in force a new Criminal Code which is in the same text for the general part and in this special part as it was before, but with some new text which is in accordance with the new treaties, with the new situation with human law, which what is explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: That is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was the 1977 text that you adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that you didn't incorporate any amendments made by Serbia and Montenegro to that law in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: No. We incorporated some, maybe 80 per cent of the old text which is the same in old Yugoslav Criminal Code and in new Criminal Code of Serbia and Montenegro. For example, legal defence or something like that is the same text. If we compare this text, it's the same. But not the same as it is, for example, Austrian criminal law and our criminal law, but the similarity is very obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I would have one or two questions for you. At the risk of being criticised by the OTP that the law of extradition does not apply in whatever way, I nevertheless would like to ask you the following: The prohibition against re-extradition is part of the rule of speciality. Is that a correct understanding? The rule of speciality seems to be more or less well established customary law. Do you agree with that? Yes. Would you also agree, it's just a question, that where someone is extradited with his consent by expeditious procedures or whatever but then still being an extradition, that then the rule of speciality under various systems and in some international treaties would not be applicable anymore? That means that consent of the extraditee, that that would -- has as a consequence the loss of the protection of the rule of speciality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I have to confess, Your Honour, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think that additional research would have to be done. However, I don't think that the rule of speciality is the rule which grants rights to the extraditee, to the person who is extradited. It's a rule which applies between the surrendering state and the requesting state. That is my first reaction. And I would think then that despite the fact that a person voluntarily surrendered to another state, the rule of speciality could apply, although in the very essence of extradition is not voluntary surrender. In the very essence of extradition is an exercise of the authority of the surrendering state transferring the person concerned to another state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it then true that if someone consents to be extradited that the coercion by the state is not the vital issue any more but the will of the person concerned to stand trial or to serve a sentence abroad that becomes the vital issue and that the coercion of the state goes to the background?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: What I think, and I refer now to your example from before of a person who went to Spain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Spain to Italy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: There is a difference. A person who went from France to Spain and there was arrested and then surrendered to Italy, went there without expectation first that he would be tried in Spain, and second he went there without the expectation that he will be surrendered to a third state, and in that sense there is no reason for -- to grant him a benefit of this reasonable expectation. Now, a person who voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal, surrendered in order to be tried here in The Hague and not -- he -- I believe that none of the persons who surrendered to the Tribunal, or most of them, never had an idea that they would be transferred to another state, and this -- and at the same time they had the confidence in the court. They showed this confidence by surrendering. And I don't think that this confidence would exist if they knew that they would be then transferred to a third state. And I think there is -- this is an essential difference between re-extradition in the sense of voluntarily -- of a person voluntarily going to another state and then being re-extradited to a third state and the case of person voluntarily surrendering to the Tribunal. This is a gap between those two situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Then we have entered a totally different realm, and that is the realm not of a state putting conditions but the realm of persons expecting something as a result of their own behaviour, which is of course totally different from extradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: We have -- we have these expectations from the -- on the side of the accused. However, we have a number of considerations from -- coming from international customary law. We are not saying that the rule against the re-extradition is automatically applicable as such. We are saying that we have a situation which is so similar to a re-extradition that the rule of re-extradition which is widely accepted among the states - it's part of international customary law - should apply and should be a consideration at least for the Bench in the present case, because it's part of international law and it's part of the law that is applied by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, totally different subject, a very short question. Could you provide the Chamber with your provisions, your legal provisions on the applicability of the criminal law in time and space? Do you understand what I mean? The jurisdiction of principles applied. And could you perhaps just in one or two words tell us, since Vukovar is not the territory of present Serbia and Montenegro, what would be the possible jurisdictional basis to try the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I believe -- just a second. I'm just going to try finding the provision. Not to retell it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you all being Serbian origin that you know your law and that you'll not be surprised if the Chamber would at this stage ask for these legal provisions, and I hope that you, Professor Horvatic, would not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I would say there are two bases of jurisdiction. One is provided in our criminal law is also provided in the criminal law applicable in the case, 1993's version of the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: And it is Article 106, saying that Yugoslav criminal law is applicable to a national of Yugoslavia, also in the case when he commits a criminal offence abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Principle of nationality. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other basis would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other one would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: The other is contained -- and we don't have a practice on that. This is a new law on war crimes much and in its Article 2, and we mentioned this Article in our written submission. The law says: "This law shall be applicable for the purpose of, among other things, of criminal prosecution and trying for grave violations of international humanitarian law committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1 January 1991, which are set forth in the statute of the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you adopted more or less our jurisdictional basis. If I were an accused could I defend myself by saying that this law could not be retroactively applied and therefore it's very important for those who commit --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: For the first situation the issue of retroactivity does not arise. The criminal law would be applicable then. For this situation the issue of retroactivity will arise and then we will have the whole discussion on the applicability of international law which was raised in the Prosecutor's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would clarify the meaning of "national of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: National of Yugoslavia would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have jurisdiction over Croatian Croats who committed their crime in Croatian. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. We could also -- we have a provision on basic universal jurisdiction in our Criminal Code. If you ask me to define Yugoslav national, this is a person having Yugoslav nationality at the time the offence was committed, presumably. However, there is a universal jurisdiction provision, so we could try -- with certain conditions we could try such a person before our courts under the criminal law of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noticed Professor Horvatic has something. No. He is withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have 15 minutes left. I would like to give seven and a half minutes to Defence and seven and a half minutes to the Prosecution. Perhaps the Prosecution first because they filed the motion. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to inform the Bench, we were able to distribute to the Defence counsel as ordered one part of the submission which is the actual response and if we can be assisted by the -- by our colleague, the usher, the other parts. I wanted to bring to the Bench's attention Article 110 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which is referred to in our submission which was applicable at the time of the commission of the offences, criminal codes of republics and autonomous provinces apply to anybody who on the territory of the republic or autonomous province commits a criminal act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a good guess. In general, we'd very much like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Texts of legal provisions are provided to the interpreters' booth when quoted, but if you would slowly --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will just draw attention to provision 2. It is the law of the republic or autonomous province in which the act has been committed that shall be applied. If the interpreters need it, I'm happy to provide it. My apologies. We didn't realise that it would be invoked at this particular hearing. The -- the Prosecution will not reiterate comments. We think that we have -- in making our request directed to two states, we have put this squarely in front of the Referral Bench for its determination. We think that the arguments have been full and that the concerns as to which of the two, if any, if the Chamber is minded to make the referral, which of the two would be the most appropriate forum. We will restrict legal argument to that which has been already before the Chamber in submissions. I do note that there had been discussion earlier about the applicability of principles ever customary law hovering over statutory law and that the ECHR and the ICCPR would not look necessarily unfavourably on perhaps some degree of retroactivity where that -- where those provisions that are at issue are covered by customary law. Again, I believe the citations -- well, they should have been provided, but the -- let me just see if I can get it to you real quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps while you're trying to find it, I noted, Ms. Somers, that the Prosecution comes then with two solutions of what should be done if there was not direct applicability of the -- and self-execution of the treaty provisions. I also noticed, but I know you've got a few minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to cover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also noted that might not resolve the problem because what then should be enacted in the view of the OTP might create a similar problem of retroactivity -- retroactive applicability of the provisions that the OTP thinks should be enacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just the 'Chambers' attention to our submission of 28 April paragraph 19, and which cites to Article 15, paragraph (ii) of the ICCPR and of the footnote that is incorporated therein is citing to Article 72 of the ECHR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution will not have any additional comment. I think if the Chamber has any further question of us, we're happy to respond. But I think we've covered our points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I will grant to the Defence the two and a half extra minutes that the Prosecution left you. I don't know who is going to -- Mr. Vasic. It's you or are you splitting up the tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will address you very briefly, and my colleagues will also use the opportunity to address you. First I wish to respond to what my learned friend said just a while ago about the application of Article 110 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. It seems to me that this refers to crimes provided for by republican law whereas we are now dealing with the SFRY Criminal Code. This is not the same code. I also wish to use the opportunity to respond to what Professor Horvatic said in connection with the existence of an indictment before the county court in Vukovar against the accused in this case. You will find in the court records that on two occasions within six months attempts were made to deliver the indictment of the county court of Vukovar to the accused in the Detention Unit and there is no doubt that criminal proceedings are being conducted against him there. It will be easy for the Court to check this. I also wish to say something about the issue of extradition. I wish to point ought that in cases of voluntary surrender by the accused, one must bear in mind that it took place only after the enactment of the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal through the mediation of the state and based on the law. For this reason, the Defence submits that this voluntary surrender must be harmonised with all the rules governing the transfer of the accused by the state based on international treaties. Therefore, we abide by our claim that the rules governing extradition should be applied in this case. Thank you, Your Honours. Those are my arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I only wish to stress that the primary principle that we must respect is the principle of a fair trial. All the arguments put forward by the Prosecutor's office and the various sides are something we have heard and I will not repeat. But to me it seems that all the arguments pertaining to a fair trial are in favour of a trial in Belgrade. The OSCE report that we have mentioned support the claim that a fair trial could not be held in Croatia with all due respect to the courts and judges there for the reasons we have mentioned. I will conclude by saying that today a case before the county court in Vukovar, which is being actively prosecuted, is the case against the accused sitting here in this courtroom. In any case, when the Trial Chamber reads the OSCE report of the 26th of April, 2005, I think the Chamber will accept the arguments of the Defence that a fair trial can be held only in Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this has been very expeditious on the part of all my colleagues and learned friends. I will try to be as expeditious as they have been. I only wish to touch upon two issues. One was raised more than once by Ms. Somers during this hearing, and it refers to the principle of conducting the proceedings in the place where the crimes took place, and this truly is a universal principle. However, I wish to refer to the arguments put forward in paragraphs 8 to 21 of our initial submission. Something that the Prosecutor said puts me in a rather special situation, and that is the Prosecutor's standpoint that this is primarily because of closeness to the victims, and this is true and has been also said by the President of the Tribunal in connection international justice. This aspect of relation of victims to the proceedings when viewed in the context of international law is open to discussion. We can, for example, point to examples of ethnic cleansing. The Ademi, Norac case, there has been a motion to refer it to Croatia, but the victims are no longer in Croatia. Where are they? There is another case where 40 victims arrived as witnesses for the Prosecution in Samac municipality where 90 per cent of the victims no longer live. I draw attention to these examples in order to underline the fact that when international times are being considered, all this has to be taken into account and special considerations have to be taken on board. There is no doubt that an attorney can sit, and I'm referring now to the representation of the accused in Croatia, that an attorney from another country can sit beside the lead counsel, but what is at stake here is the relationship of trust and confidence between the accused and his lead counsel. And as these are civilian, military, and security structures, it will be very hard to establish a relationship of full confidence. Your Honours, our clients have pleaded not guilty. They have not pleaded guilty to the crimes they are charged with. Our professional task as Defence counsel is to focus all our professional activity on demonstrating that they are not guilty. For this we need two things, due process and facts and evidence that will allow us to challenge the Prosecutor's arguments and demonstrate the innocence of our clients. The facts and evidence are a matter for the Defence to come up with, but due process and a fair trial has to be provided for by the Court. We are nothing more and nothing less of you, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. This concludes the hearing of today. It's not the first 11 bis hearing before this Chamber, but especially where the motion was filed with an open choice to refer the case to Croatia or to Serbia and Montenegro, the Chamber, of course, is confronted with an additional issue, and that is where to send the case. It could be no surprise if victims or relative -- relatives of victims would prefer to have their cases tried before courts of their own state, because they might fear that if the case would be heard in a state where the accused are nationals of, that perhaps not sufficient weight would be given to their interests and too much weight to the interests of the accused. Whereas on the other hand, the accused might have fear that if they are tried in the state of the victims that too much weight would be given to the interests of the victims and that their rights would not be sufficiently guaranteed. That is at least one of the issues, apart from all the others we discussed, which this Referral Chamber is confronted with. I'd like to thank the parties for their submissions. That certainly will assist the Chamber in making the determination the Chamber would have to make. And I would also like very much to thank the representatives of the governments of Serbia and Montenegro and of Croatia for the assistance they have provided to the Chamber. We stand adjourned.
